clue.text: Might win at poker-result of good play ?

blocks.note: first meaning: a poker hand of three of a kind plus a pair
second meaning: a theatre with every seat sold after a well-reviewed production

explanation.surface: A card player reflects that skilful play brings victory at the poker table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good play' reads as skill at cards, but it is a good stage play that packs the theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names both a strong poker hand that often takes the pot and a theatre audience with every seat taken.

clue.text: Jocose view on monetary obligations

blocks.note: a facet is one aspect or view of a matter
IOUs are written promises to repay money

explanation.surface: A light-hearted opinion about debts.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed above: the view sits on top of the obligations.
explanation.definitionFit: Jocose and facetious are synonyms, both meaning joking and flippant in manner.

clue.text: Let down by milk supplier ?

blocks.note: first meaning: to bring down, rhyming with mower
second meaning: something that lows or moos, a cow, rhyming with slower

explanation.surface: Disappointed by the dairy that delivers the milk.
explanation.walkthrough: The two meanings are pronounced differently: one rhymes with grower, the other is a whimsical name for a mooing cow.
explanation.definitionFit: To lower a rope is to let it down, and a cow that lows, or moos, supplies milk.

clue.text: What the drunk said about the girl being Greek

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the other

blocks.note: hic is the hiccup of a drunk
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A drunk man is muttering about a Greek girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What the drunk said' sounds like reported speech, but it is the drunk's hiccup, which wraps round the girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Hellenic means relating to Greece or the ancient Greeks, from Hellas, their own name for the country.

clue.text: Sole connection with a number of top people

blocks.note: a shoe's upper is the part joined to the sole
ten is a number

explanation.surface: A footwear manufacturer has links with several important people.
explanation.walkthrough: The upper ten (short for upper ten thousand) is an old phrase for the aristocracy.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase was coined for the wealthiest ten thousand in New York and came to mean the social elite generally.

clue.text: Leave out former church training

blocks.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
CE is the Church of England
PT is physical training

explanation.surface: Skip the physical exercise that the church used to hold.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, except means to exclude or omit, as in present company excepted.

clue.text: Many wise to back this artist

indicators.note: putting a word to the back, turning it rearward, means reading it from its end to its start

blocks.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500, a crossword stand-in for many
sage means wise

explanation.surface: Plenty of knowledgeable people would back this painter's work.
explanation.walkthrough: D stays put and SAGE runs backwards after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgar Degas was the French Impressionist painter famous for his ballet dancers.

clue.text: American stations of foreign vessels

blocks.note: de is French for of
pots are vessels for cooking or holding liquid

explanation.surface: US ports where ships from abroad dock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foreign vessels' looks like overseas ships, but 'of foreign' is the French word de.
explanation.definitionFit: In the United States a depot is a railway or bus station, not just a storehouse.

clue.text: Clothes laid out, including one blouse

indicators.note: including means holding inside, so one piece sits within the other
out here means put out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: garb means clothes
I is the Roman numeral one
the letters of laid rearranged

explanation.surface: Garments set out ready to wear, a blouse among them.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes inside GARB to make GARIB, which comes before the rearranged letters of laid.
explanation.definitionFit: A garibaldi is a loose red blouse for women, modelled on the shirts of Garibaldi's followers.

clue.text: Plant by beginning of spring, on border

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of spring
an edge is a border

explanation.surface: A gardener puts something in as spring starts, along the flower border.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedge is a grass-like plant that grows in wet ground, often by rivers and marshes.

clue.text: Flower is a feature in Jersey, perhaps?

blocks.note: first meaning: a yellow spring wild flower
second meaning, split in two: a facial feature of a Jersey, the dairy breed

explanation.surface: A particular flower is a notable sight on the island of Jersey.
explanation.walkthrough: Jersey looks like the Channel Island, but it is the breed of cow; 'perhaps' warns that it is one example of a cow. Read the answer as COW'S LIP.
explanation.definitionFit: The cowslip is a common European primula with nodding yellow flowers, and a cow's lip is part of any Jersey's face.

clue.text: Skipped poor opening in C. Reade novel

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, so only that one is kept
novel means new and original, so the letters are made into something new

blocks.note: the first letter of poor
the initial and surname taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone skipped the weak first chapter of a book by the Victorian novelist Charles Reade.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Reade wrote The Cloister and the Hearth, so 'C. Reade novel' reads as a book title; 'novel' is the anagram signal, with P put in among the name's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To caper is to leap and dance about playfully, which is a lively form of skipping.

clue.text: This card trick isn't seen at the bridge table

definitions.text: This card trick isn't seen at the bridge table

blocks.note: surface reading: a sleight-of-hand card trick, a con with cards

blocks.clueFragment: isn't seen at the bridge table
blocks.note: setter's reading: the missing word joins card trick to name the swindle, and a bridge trick always holds four cards, never fewer

explanation.surface: A cardsharp's dodge is never attempted among respectable bridge players.
explanation.walkthrough: Put the answer before 'card trick' to name the find-the-lady swindle; at bridge every trick has four cards, so a trick of this size never happens there.
explanation.definitionFit: The three-card trick is the street gambling con where a punter must find the queen among a trio of cards.

clue.text: Of good character, but could be replaced?

blocks.note: first meaning: well thought of, respectable
second meaning: able to be put back again

explanation.surface: A respectable employee who nevertheless might be dismissed and swapped for another.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a coined split word: re (again) + put + able, so 'able to be put back'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone reputable enjoys a good reputation, which is what having good character amounts to.

clue.text: Unlikely to win, our diet's upset him

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase for a noun: a contestant who is unlikely to win

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A trainer explains that a poor feeding regime has left the horse with little chance.
explanation.definitionFit: In racing an outsider is a horse or competitor given long odds, one not expected to finish first.

clue.text: Poem could be Milton's? No. Kipling's

indicators.note: could be says these letters might become something else once rearranged

blocks.note: the letters taken as written, punctuation ignored

explanation.surface: Is this verse by Milton? No, it was written by Kipling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kipling's' completes the definition: the poem is Kipling's ballad of a soul turned away from both Heaven and Hell.
explanation.definitionFit: Tomlinson is a narrative poem by Rudyard Kipling, published in Barrack-Room Ballads in 1892.

clue.text: Strike in mine about money

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the other

blocks.note: to sap is to dig a mine or trench under a fortification
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Miners walk out over pay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike in mine' paints an industrial dispute; strike is the definition, and mine is a verb meaning to dig under defences.
explanation.definitionFit: A slap is a blow with the open hand, so to slap someone is to strike them.

clue.text: Splendid display for a time in home store

indicators.note: in places one word inside another

blocks.note: a pantry is the room at home where food is stored
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A shop window set out handsomely for a while in a household goods store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home store' looks like a shop selling household goods; it is the cupboard room in a house where food is kept.
explanation.definitionFit: Pageantry is elaborate ceremonial show, splendour put on for spectacle.

clue.text: Article rewritten about northern musical instrument

indicators.note: something rewritten is put into a new form, so the letters are reordered
about means around, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: the letters of article rearranged
N is the abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: A newspaper feature is revised to cover a folk instrument from the north.
explanation.definitionFit: The clarinet is a single-reed woodwind instrument with a cylindrical bore.

clue.text: Raising of money on 2 by an adherent

indicators.note: in a down clue raising a word lifts it upwards, so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: the word of, read upwards
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra
the answer to 2 down

explanation.surface: Fundraising for clue 2 by a supporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raising of money' reads as fundraising, but only 'of' is turned up; 'on' in a down clue puts the money above the answer to 2.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower is a disciple or supporter, the same thing as an adherent of a cause.

clue.text: Part of problem for speakers

indicators.note: what speakers hear is the sound of the word, not its spelling

blocks.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem

explanation.surface: One element of a difficulty facing public speakers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of problem' looks like a hidden-word signal, but 'Part of' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Some means a portion of, as in some of the cake, which is a part of the whole.

clue.text: Admitting total indebtedness

blocks.note: all means the total, the whole lot
owing means being in debt

explanation.surface: A borrower confesses to the full extent of what they owe.
explanation.definitionFit: Allowing a point in argument is conceding or granting it, the same as admitting it.

clue.text: Call our attention to an opening ?

blocks.note: hi is a call of greeting
directed at us, wanting our attention

explanation.surface: Drawing the public's notice to a newly opened shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as 'Hi! At us!', a call that seeks our attention.
explanation.definitionFit: A hiatus is a gap or break in a series, so it is an opening in the sense of a space.

clue.text: The late rower

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who has died, or someone behind time
setter's reading: a rower whose passengers are the late, the dead, ferried across the Styx

explanation.surface: An obituary note for an oarsman who has recently died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The late' looks like a mark of respect for a dead oarsman; in fact the dead are the ones he carries.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this ferryman rows the souls of the dead across the River Styx to Hades for a coin.

clue.text: Native scattered this in bush

indicators.note: things scattered are thrown about out of order
in places one word inside another

blocks.note: the letters of this rearranged
a brier is a thorny bush such as the wild rose

explanation.surface: Local people scattered something in the undergrowth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Native' looks like an adjective about the bush, but it is the definition: a person born in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A Britisher is a native of Britain, a word used chiefly by Americans.

clue.text: Some probe vindicates a Labour statesman ?

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only a part of it, a run of letters within

blocks.note: the run spanning the end of probe and the start of vindicates

explanation.surface: An inquiry clears the name of a Labour politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Ernest Bevin was a trade union leader and the post-war Labour Foreign Secretary.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernest Bevin served as Minister of Labour under Churchill and Foreign Secretary under Attlee.

clue.text: Creeper put back by a fastener

indicators.note: putting something back sends it the other way, so the word is read in reverse

blocks.note: a nail fastens things together
taken as written

explanation.surface: A climbing plant has been fixed back in place with a clip.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed fastener comes first, then A: 'by' just means next to.
explanation.definitionFit: A liana is a long woody climbing vine of tropical forests, a creeper in the plant sense.

clue.text: Bell's produced it in the island

blocks.note: first meaning, split in two: what a bell gives out when rung slowly
second meaning: a ring-shaped coral island

explanation.surface: A church bell has been rung somewhere on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as A TOLL: the sound a bell makes.
explanation.definitionFit: An atoll is a ring of coral reef and islets around a lagoon, a type of island.

clue.text: He calls for it in a mask

indicators.note: in places one word inside another

blocks.note: a visor is a mask or the face guard of a helmet
taken as written

explanation.surface: A masked man shouts for something; perhaps a game of tag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He calls for it' reads as one action, but the definition stops at 'calls': a caller is someone who calls round.
explanation.definitionFit: A visitor is someone who calls on you, paying a call at your house.

clue.text: Poet seen in another bar

blocks.note: a new one is another, a fresh one
a bolt is a bar that secures a door

explanation.surface: A poet is spotted drinking in a second pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Henry Newbolt wrote the patriotic poems Drake's Drum and Vitai Lampada (Play up! play up! and play the game!).
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Newbolt was an English poet of the late Victorian and Edwardian era.

clue.text: One enters opposing points in church office

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: north and south, opposite points of the compass
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone joins a congregation with opposing views about church office.
explanation.walkthrough: The compass points split around ONE, N first and S last.
explanation.definitionFit: Nones is the canonical hour of prayer said at the ninth hour, about three in the afternoon, one of the daily church offices.

clue.text: Aunt confused by court exchanges, of course

indicators.note: confused letters are muddled up out of their order

blocks.note: the letters of aunt rearranged
a rally is a run of strokes exchanged on a tennis court

explanation.surface: An elderly aunt is baffled by legal exchanges in a courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: Court looks like a law court, but it is the tennis court where shots are exchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: Naturally and of course are interchangeable sentence adverbs meaning as anyone would expect.
